newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Time running out for Albanian elections - minister.
newsitem.headline: Time running out for Albanian elections - minister.

text.p: Albania's justice minister said on Monday time was running out for holding elections as planned by June and called on parties in the national reconciliation government to agree quickly on the form of the vote.
"Politicians should be more reasonable, get rid of their passions and try to reach a gentlemen's agreement where all the parties may profit," Spartak Ngjela told a news conference.
The 10-party government, formed on March 9 as a response to widespread unrest in the Balkan nation, cannot agree over what type of voting system to use.

President Sali Berisha's Democratic Party, which agreed to share power as popular anger over fraudulent investment schemes threatened to plunge the nation into anarchy, is holding out for a first-past-the post system.
The other nine parties want some form of proportional representation.

The Democratic Party won 122 seats in the 140 seat parliament in the last general election in May 1996. Three of the parties in the national reconciliation government, including the main opposition Socialist Party, boycotted the vote saying it was rigged.
Fresh elections by June were agreed when the national reconciliation govenment was set up.

Ngjela, an independent close to the monarchist party, said parties in the government should agree within the next two days on one of the two drafts of the electoral law so that it could be passed by parliament by May 15.
"May 15th is the final limit when the law should be passed by the parliament, if we are to hold elections in June...The consensus should be reached in the next two days," he said.

Berisha is also pressing for the dissolution of the salvation committees, citizens' groups that sprung up across the south as Albanians furious at the loss of their savings in the pyramid investment schemes looted military arsenals and created near anarchy.
More than 300 people have died in the violence and unofficial estimates say up to a million light weapons have been distributed among Albania's 3.4 million people.

Berisha says that while the salvation committees remain, there cannot be free and fair elections. The committees, who blame the president for the collapse of the pyramid schemes, control much of the south.
"The conflict is more political than juridical," Ngjela said.

The justice minister suggested that the impasse might be resolved with the help of outside agents, an apparant reference to the Italians, who head an eight-nation force of 6,000 troops sent to Albania to secure deliveries of humanitarian aid.
"I think that with the intervention of the guaranteeing forces...something will be achieved," he said.
"All society wants to have elections by June and the international community is committed to the end of June."
